China may be set to overtake the United States in the next decade as the world's second largest consumer of luxury goods, but the question remains whether China's new money will put their yuan behind products made -- let alone designed -- in their own backyard. 
''China Design Now,'' at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London through July 13, takes an expansive view of China's burgeoning design culture. 
Still, the fact that the curators saw fit to include projects like Rem Koolhaas's CCTV headquarters and Herzog & de Meuron's Olympic stadium as well as a pair of Nike Air Force 1's could be taken as a hint. 
Meanwhile, the KT Wong Charitable Trust has commissioned the Chinese artist Shao Fan to create a garden for the Royal Horticultural Society Chelsea Flower Show in May. 
Fan's design (above, right), which brings a contemporary perspective to the traditional scholar's garden, is an elegant example of the Wong Trust's ambition to foster an East/West exchange of a decidedly more cerebral nature.

file: Sites for the Socially Conscious.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE are many Web sites devoted to criticizing industries and companies. 
Many are of the ''Wal-Mart Watch'' variety (walmartwatch.com) and are decidedly one-sided.
There are also services like the Dow Jones sustainability indexes (www.sustainability-indexes.com), and the many sites for ''socially conscious'' investors. 
These, according to a recent article in The Harvard Business Review, amount to a ''cacophony of self-appointed scorekeepers'' that make up a ''jumble of largely meaningless rankings, allowing almost any company to boast that it meets some measure of social responsibility.''
Now comes Do The Right Thing (dotherightthing.com), a site introduced this month. 
It works like Digg.com in having users make submissions, which are then voted on by readers. 
''All are welcome,'' the site announces, including ''people who buy the stuff, who make the stuff, who live in communities where the stuff is made, and who have transcendent abilities to speak on behalf of that which cannot speak (like wildlife and the environment).''
Once companies are submitted, they are evaluated for 60 days. 
Users submit evidence for or against the company, votes are tallied, and a ''social performance'' score is given. 
After the initial evaluation, the score can still change with further submissions and voting.
''Its important to create a system that has a balance of accountability and free form,'' Ryan Mickle, the site's founder, told David Cohn of newassignment.net. 
It is based on Digg, he said, because ''it's a balance between a wiki and a forum, and neither [alone] would have worked for Do The Right Thing.''
This may not yield a fully balanced assessment of every company, but only time will tell that. 
While it seems at least possible that most users will be predisposed to take a negative view of a given company, the site is open to people with all points of view.
''Google does EVIL by allowing censorship in China,'' is the headline on one recent submission, which referred to an article on TechCrunch.com. 
But the article was about a Google founder, Sergey Brin, recently expressing regret over Google's earlier decision to allow China to censor its search results. 
When several other users pointed this out to the submitter, he referred to a different article about Chinese censorship that referred to Google only peripherally. 
Most users gave the post a thumbs-down, and it ended up with a below-zero score. 
Still, as of Thursday, 67 users had voted positively on the submission, essentially agreeing that it should count against Google.
One user questions the very nature of the site, asserting that it is based on false premises. 
Many things companies do, this user noted, have both good and bad consequences. 
Should complicated matters really be measured with a simple thumbs-up or down?
''Is outsourcing really not the right thing?'' he asked. 
''Are you sure?''
The user concluded, ''I recommend using and posting to this site with trepidation.''
That, and perhaps not writing off those ''self-appointed scorekeepers'' so quickly.CREDIT SCORE MISTAKES -- People trying to repair their credit often operate from ignorance of how credit scores are determined. 
For them, the Simple Dollar (thesimpledollar.com) offers the ''10 Common Tactical Mistakes When Dealing With The Credit Score Blues.''
For instance, canceling old credit cards is not always a good idea, because the length of a person's credit history is a big factor on a credit score. 
Also, the site advises, ''if you have balances on other cards, canceling an old credit card can also worsen your debt ratio, which makes up 30 percent of your score.''DEDUCTIVE REASONING -- Bankrate.com offers the wild and the wacky from the world of tax deductions. 
More than one person has tried to write off the cost of day care for a dog. 
One Amish man wanted to write off his buggy, on which he had spent about $1,000 to install dashboard lights, kickplates, a tinted windshield and a velvet interior. 
Not all offbeat deductions are illegal, though. 
One man successfully wrote off his comic-book collection because he wrote his doctoral thesis on the societal impact of comics. 
DAN MITCHELLComplete links are at nytimes.com/business.

file: Skype Text Is Monitored In China.txt
text:
ï»¿
SAN FRANCISCO -- A group of Canadian human-rights activists and computer security researchers has discovered a huge surveillance system in China that monitors and archives certain Internet text conversations that include politically charged words.
The system tracks text messages sent by customers of Tom-Skype, a joint venture between a Chinese wireless operator and eBay, the Web auctioneer that owns Skype, an online phone and text messaging service.
The discovery draws more attention to the Chinese government's Internet monitoring and filtering efforts, which created controversy this summer during the Beijing Olympics. 
Researchers in China have estimated that 30,000 or more ''Internet police'' monitor online traffic, Web sites and blogs for political and other offending content in what is called the Golden Shield Project or the Great Firewall of China.
The activists, who are based at Citizen Lab, a research group that focuses on politics and the Internet at the University of Toronto, discovered the surveillance operation last month. 
They said a cluster of eight message-logging computers in China contained more than a million censored messages. 
They examined the text messages and reconstructed a list of restricted words.
The list includes words related to the religious group Falun Gong, Taiwan independence and the Chinese Communist Party, according to the researchers. 
It includes not only words like democracy, but also earthquake and milk powder. 
(Chinese officials are facing criticism over the handling of earthquake relief and chemicals tainting milk powder.)
The list also serves as a filter to restrict text conversations. 
The encrypted list of words inside the Tom-Skype software blocks the transmission of those words and a copy of the message is sent to a server. 
The Chinese servers retained personal information about the customers who sent the messages. 
They also recorded chat conversations between Tom-Skype users and Skype users outside China. 
The system recorded text messages and Skype caller identification, but did not record the content of Skype voice calls.
In just two months, the servers archived more than 166,000 censored messages from 44,000 users, according to a report that was published on the Information Warfare Monitor Web site at the university.
The researchers were able to download and analyze copies of the surveillance data because the Chinese computers were improperly configured, leaving them accessible. 
The researchers said they did not know who was operating the surveillance system, but they said they suspected that it was the Chinese wireless firm, possibly with cooperation from Chinese police.
Independent executives from the instant message industry say the discovery is an indication of a spiraling computer war that is tracking the introduction of new communications technologies.
''I can see an arms race going on,'' said Pat Peterson, vice president for technology at Cisco's Ironport group, which provides messaging security systems. 
''China is one of the more wired places of the world and they are fighting a war with their populace.''
The Chinese government is not alone in its Internet surveillance efforts. 
In 2005, The New York Times reported that the National Security Agency was monitoring large volumes of telephone and Internet communications flowing into and out of the United States as part of the eavesdropping program, intended to hunt for evidence of terrorist activity, that President Bush approved after the Sept. 
11 attacks.
The researchers said their discovery contradicted a public statement made by Skype executives in 2006 after the content filtering of the Skype conversations was reported. 
At the time the company said that the conversations were protected and private.
The Citizen Lab researchers issued a report on Wednesday, which details an analysis of data on the servers. 
''We were able to download millions of messages that identify users,'' said Ronald J. Deibert, an associate professor of political science at the University of Toronto. 
''This is the worst nightmares of the conspiracy theorists around surveillance coming true. 
It's 'X-Files' without the aliens.''
Jennifer Caukin, an eBay spokeswoman, said, ''The security and privacy of our users is very important to Skype.''
But the company spoke to the accessibility of the messages, not their monitoring. 
''The security breach does not affect Skype's core technology or functionality,'' she said. 
''It exists within an administrative layer on Tom Online servers. 
We have expressed our concern to Tom Online about the security issue and they have informed us that a fix to the problem will be completed within 24 hours.''
EBay had no comment on the monitoring.
Other American companies have been caught in controversy after cooperating with Chinese officials. 
In 2005, Yahoo supplied information to the Chinese authorities, who then sentenced a reporter, Shi Tao, to 10 years in prison for leaking what the government considered state secrets. 
The company said it was following Chinese law.
EBay created the joint venture with the Tom Group, which holds the majority stake, in September 2005. 
The Tom Group itself was founded in October 1999 as a joint venture among Hutchison Whampoa, Cheung Kong Holdings and other investors. 
In its annual report this year, the Tom Group, based in Hong Kong, said that the number of Tom-Skype registered users had reached 69 million in the first half of 2008 and revenue had increased tenfold in the last year.
The researchers stumbled upon the surveillance system when Nart Villeneuve, a senior research fellow at Citizen Lab, began using an analysis tool to monitor data that was generated by the Tom-Skype software, which is meant to permit voice and text conversations from a personal computer. 
By observing the data generated by the program, he determined that each time he typed a particular swear word into the text messaging program an encrypted message was sent to an unidentified Internet address.
To his surprise, the coded messages were being stored on Tom Online computers. 
When he examined the machines over the Internet, he discovered that they had been misconfigured and that the computer directories were readable with a simple Web browser.
One directory on each machine contained a series of files in which the messages, in encrypted form, were being deposited. 
Hunting further, Mr. Villeneuve soon found a file that contained the numerical key that permitted him to decode the encrypted log files.
What he uncovered were hundreds of files, each containing thousands of records of messages that had been captured and then stored by the filtering software. 
The records revealed Internet addresses and user names as well as message content. 
Also stored on the computers were calling records for Skype voice conversations containing names and in some cases phone numbers of the calling parties.
Mr. Villeneuve downloaded the messages, decrypted them and used machine translation software to convert the Chinese messages to English. 
He then used word frequency counts to identify the key words that were flagging the messages. 
The exact criteria used by the filtering software is still unclear, he said, because some messages on the servers contained no known key word. 
He said that in addition to capturing the Skype messages sent between Tom-Skype users, international conversations were recorded as well, meaning that users of standard Skype software outside China were also vulnerable to the surveillance system when they had text conversations with Chinese users.

file: So Many Hepatitis Cases, So Many Cures.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dr. Sing Chan, a hepatologist in Flushing, Queens, has been getting more and more invitations for lunch lately from pharmaceutical representatives seeking to interest him in new drugs developed to treat the hepatitis B virus.
As the number of new cases reaches a staggeringly high rate among recent Chinese immigrants in New York City, drug companies are descending upon doctors and pharmacists; marketers of fancy herbal remedies are pushing their products on Chinese radio; and the many shops along Flushing's Main Street that sell traditional Chinese herbs are stocking products with natural ingredients that claim to purify the liver.
A study released this week reported that east Asian immigrants in New York City run a far greater risk than other Americans for the hepatitis B virus. 
The study, led by researchers at the New York University School of Medicine, was certainly not news to Dr. Chan, whose client list has come to be dominated by Chinese immigrants living around Main Street in whom the virus has been detected.
The virus, which can lead to diseases like liver cancer and cirrhosis, has plagued Asian immigrants for decades, and the number of patients who test positive for it keeps rising in areas like Flushing.
''The numbers are going up all the time,'' Dr. Chan said. 
''Doctors are just not doing enough to test patients for hepatitis B. Infected patients tell me, 'I've had plenty of blood tests but they never checked for hepatitis B.'
''
Because hepatitis B is endemic in many Asian countries, where it is transmitted largely from mother to child, growth in the number of Asian immigrants in New York and across the country has made the disease a broad, expensive health problem. 
In the 2000 census, there were 800,000 Asians in the city, with roughly half from China.
Hepatitis B, like hepatitis C, is generally contracted through the blood, and is not transmitted through casual contact with infected people. 
Hepatitis A, which is caused by a different virus, can be transmitted through food, but hepatitis B cannot, with very rare exceptions.
''They spent one day teaching us about this in medical school,'' Dr. Chan said. 
But now doctors and authorities can not ignore the scores of patients flocking to the modest medical clinics and offices tucked away in commercial suites just off Main Street, above noodle shops, bubble tea lounges and karaoke bars.
Dr. Chan and his colleagues in Flushing are frustrated. 
They are scrambling to introduce a reluctant population of recent Chinese immigrants to medical advances in treatment of the virus, including early detection and medication that can suppress it.
''New patients say they are shocked when they find out they have the virus,'' he said. 
''Then they admit that many of their friends and relatives have it. 
You get a lot of old people who come and know they have it, but they say, 'My doctor always said nothing can be done for it.'
''
That is no longer so. 
Over the past decade, an array of new drugs has become available to treat chronic infection and suppress the virus so that it causes little or no harm. 
Usually, they must be taken for a lifetime.
''When I tell young Chinese people they have to take a lifetime worth of drugs for a virus that is currently giving them no symptoms, they don't understand that,'' he said. 
''Then they refuse and they remain carriers and can pass the virus on.''
For many Chinese immigrants, he said, hepatitis B has long carried a stigma. 
Many people were told it is incurable and not to speak about it for fear one would be vilified as a carrier.
''A lot of people don't want to come forward because they are undocumented and can't get health insurance,'' said Ming-der Chang, vice president of Asian initiatives for the American Cancer Society, which reports high incidence of liver cancer among Asian immigrants in New York City. 
''They don't want to be seen as carriers of the virus.''
A 45-year-old man who emigrated from China 10 years ago said he avoided being tested for the virus because he lacked money and health insurance. 
Getting a hepatitis B diagnosis would mean a stigma that would affect his ability to rent a room, get work and make friends, he said.
''I was worried I would be discriminated against,'' said the man, who was granted anonymity because of his illegal status and his reluctance to reveal to his friends that he has hepatitis B. ''People still think the virus can be spread by food and contact. 
Many poor immigrants come and live close together in small rooms and don't want to live close to someone who has it.''
In January 2005, the man developed liver cancer, caused by untreated hepatitis B, doctors told him. 
A yearlong regimen of chemotherapy has shrunk his tumors to the point where his doctors are optimistic about his survival, he said.
Dr. King-Chen Hon, a gastroenterologist with an office on Main Street, said that a steady stream of new patients now come in complaining of the virus. 
By then, they are yellow from jaundice or have liver problems, including cirrhosis or cancer. 
But many come in with no clue that they are infected and no real symptoms. 
Then they test positive.
Dr. Pat Basu, a hepatologist in Forest Hills, Queens, said there is a high incidence of hepatitis B among the Bukharan immigrants who live near his office. 
There is also a high rate among the South Asian populations of Indians, Pakistanis and Bengalis in Elmhurst and Bukharans in Forest Hills, doctors there say.
But it is among Chinese immigrants that the numbers are highest. 
The study found that 15 percent of east Asians in New York -- as many as 100,000 people -- are chronic hepatitis carriers, an infection rate 35 times the rate found in the general population.
Some people with hepatitis B cannot afford Western medicine or had no success with it, and turn to traditional Chinese herbal medicine, seeking to restore their health among the pungent aromas of the stores that sell lotus seeds, ginseng root, ginkgo, shark cartilage and fish oil.
Sam Zhang, 33, walked into one such store on Main Street and browsed among the glass jars of dried fish, seahorses and hundreds of varieties of tea. 
He bought $200 worth of herbal liver purifier for his mother, Li, 53, who has hepatitis B. He bought a month's supply of an herbal remedy to purify the liver, for $200.
''Our doctor said not to try any traditional Chinese medicine because it's not approved by the F.D.A.,'' said Mr. Zhang, who emigrated from Fujian Province in 1990 and owns a restaurant in Flushing. 
''But nothing else worked, so we'll give it a try.''

text:
ï»¿
BORSCHT. It's not a dish many people associate with Hong Kong, and probably not what most would order for dinner their first night in this former British colony. 
Roast pork, sure. 
A whole fish steamed with ginger, absolutely. 
But beet soup?
It hardly seems Chinese.
Yet borscht is certainly Hong Kongese, a not uncommon sight on dinner menus and an essential component of a meal at Queen's Cafe, the dim, cozy, wood-paneled restaurant where I spent one Friday evening earlier this year. 
Opened in 1952 by White Russian emigres and immortalized in the 1991 Wong Kar-wai movie ''Days of Being Wild,'' the cafe was filled with a cross-section of Hong Kong: hip kids in black glasses and cowboy boots, office workers embarking on the weekend, and first-daters, all tucking into roast chicken, rib-eye steaks, shrimp cocktail and bowls of that tangy borscht.
I was there alone, and so I brooded over my prix fixe meal of borscht and ''sharshlik'' fillet -- garlicky and a little overcooked, just the way I like it -- which cost 128 Hong Kong dollars, or $16.45 at 7.77 Hong Kong dollars to the U.S. dollar, plus a pair of Carlsberg beers for 35 Hong Kong dollars each. 
Dining with oneself for company can be difficult in any city, more so in one as jam-packed with human beings as Hong Kong: seven million inhabit the 425 square miles of this special administrative region of China, more than two-thirds of which is rural land or protected greenspace. 
Don't think sardines; think transistors on the latest Intel chip.
Adding to the challenge was my two-day budget of $500, including lodging, which in Hong Kong can go a long way -- or nowhere at all. 
Fleabags abound, noodle soups cost next to nothing, and trendy, disposable clothes are worn by everyone under the age of 40. 
At the other end of the spectrum is the Hong Kong of the bankers, the developers, the movie stars: InterContinentals and Mandarin Orientals, glittering Louis Vuitton boutiques, and private clubs whose ''Members Only'' plaques glare at you from semisecret entrances to Art Deco skyscrapers.
I wanted to live that life, but on a rickshaw-puller's salary, and so far, I'd succeeded. 
I had checked into the Cosmopolitan, a new hotel whose clean, modern rooms occupy the former premises of the Xinhua News Agency, China's official news outlet. 
The Cosmopolitan and its infinitesimally cheaper sibling, the Cosmo, lay across the street from the Happy Valley racetrack, about 10 minutes from the Causeway Bay subway station.
Reserving two nights through hotels.com set me back $176.12, and the remainder I'd calculated at approximately 2,600 Hong Kong dollars, about $334, of which I'd spent almost nothing. 
Lunch had been a noodle soup with roast pork and wontons (23 Hong Kong dollars), and the subway trip to Central, Hong Kong's downtown (5 Hong Kong dollars), put me within walking distance of the Peak Tram, the funicular (30 Hong Kong dollars round trip) that for 118 years has heaved sightseers up steep slopes to Victoria Peak. 
Or, rather, to the Peak Galeria, where I bought bags of dried mangoes and spicy dried cuttlefish (10 Hong Kong dollars each; the latter was buy-one-get-one-free!) before marching to the real peak.
The 20-minute hike along winding Mount Austin Road took me past ritzy apartment complexes and the peaceful, deep-green Victoria Peak Garden before topping out in a plaza 1,818 feet above sea level. 
Up there, families strolled paths lined with mountain laurels and azaleas, while I looked down on the city: the 50-story apartment buildings arising from the hills; the misty harbor, stocked with ferries and container ships; the black kites wheeling lazily in the sky, sighting a rodent dinner far below.
Later that day, I received a call from Tim, a childhood friend who had been living in Hong Kong for several years. 
We met for a drink at Opia, a dark bar-restaurant that would not be out of place in New York. 
Its prices, too, struck me as familiar: 132 Hong Kong dollars for my South gin martini meant, alas, that one would be my limit. 
Still, there was always Saturday.
SHOPPING in Hong Kong is more than a pastime; it's an undertaking, a scholarly pursuit. 
There was no way I could hit every shopping district in a mere 24 hours, but I was determined to do my best. 
I began with Hollywood Road, stopping first for an airy scrambled-egg-and-corned-beef sandwich (33 Hong Kong dollars with a cup of coffee) at Tsui Wah, a hectic plastic-boothed diner that serves fish-ball noodle soup alongside baked pork chops with tomato sauce.
One of the oldest streets in Hong Kong, Hollywood Road is famous for its antiques shops, art galleries and the boutique zones of Soho and Noho. 
But the very first store I walked into was of more recent vintage: G.O.D., or Goods of Desire, a minichain that applies Hong Kong street style to Ikea-like home decor, clothing and stationery. 
Here were pajamas printed with classified ads from Chinese newspapers, Lucite frames bearing stock shots of people from the 1960's, and rather comfy-looking sofas that might have been a tad difficult to ship back home. 
(Dear G.O.D., please open a New York branch.)
On I soldiered, glancing at the contemporary Vietnamese paintings at Arch Angel Gallery (53-55 Hollywood Road) and sampling the premium men's denim at Jeanious before happening upon Wattis Fine Art, which was the host of a show of Arthur Hacker's pen-and-ink drawings of 1970's Hong Kong.
Mr. Hacker, a British writer and artist who has lived in the city since 1967, renders street life with a strong, funny, simple line, carefully tracing the flower print on a hippie's shirt or the precarious-looking bamboo scaffolding still used on construction sites today. 
No catalog was available, and the drawings cost 8,500 Hong Kong dollars and up, but a lithograph of his ''Evolution of the Hong Kong Bar Girl'' was a relative bargain at 500 Hong Kong dollars; I snapped one up.
Lunchtime!
I met my friend Fed at Isola, a trendy Italian restaurant with a magnificent harbor view and an equally magnificent set menu (218 Hong Kong dollars): an antipasto buffet (from olives to octopus salad and beyond), a main course (gnochetti al ragu, red mullet) and a dessert bar (panna cotta, fruit salad, creme brulee, chocolate mousse, apple tart ).
Over the gut-busting meal, Fed, a consummate shopper, gave me advice: Skip the glossy shops of Central, and make for Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon, Paterson Street in Causeway Bay, and the area around 3 Pacific Place in Wan Chai.
I splurged on a scenic cruise across the harbor on the Star Ferry, dropping 2.20 Hong Kong dollars for an upper-deck seat (the lower deck is 1.70). 
The ferry, in operation since 1888, has the advantage of being fast as well as atmospheric, and landed me in Tsim Sha Tsui in under 10 minutes.
For Tsim Sha Tsui bargains, there is one destination: the third floor of the Silvercord Center, where the I.T. 
Sale Shop has off-season fashions from brands like Paul Smith and Cacharel at up to 90 percent off. 
I found an A.P.C. suit down from 6,199 Hong Kong dollars to 3,100 -- cheap, but not quite frugal.
A few flights down, however, was a warren of stores operated by I.T., a fashion conglomerate with 230 shops across Greater China. 
Some sell international brands; others offer I.T.'s own labels, of which Izzue has become my favorite, seeming to take my best memories of the Gap and Urban Outfitters and give them an amusing Hong Kong twist. 
I walked out with lightweight olive-green pants and a rumpled blue-striped button-down (698 Hong Kong dollars).
After a restorative nap at the Cosmopolitan, I went in search of 3 Pacific Place and Flea n Cents, (34-38 Queen's Road East, Wan Chai) whose world-spanning collection of vintagetoys, furniture and tchotchkes Fed was certain I'd love. 
It was closed. 
A nearby Illy Cafe, however, was open, and sold a wide array of CD's -- classic reggae and soul, the new Neko Case and ''Xiang Gang Electric,'' a compilation of local D.J.'s, which I bought for 128 Hong Kong dollars.
Time for dinner. 
Again, I was alone. 
(My friend Tim works for a large newsweekly based in Hong Kong, and a breaking story kept him in the office.) But Xi Yan Sweets, a Chinese restaurant whose up-and-coming chef, Jacky Yu, takes cues from Southeast Asia, knows how to treat the solo diner. 
My waitress endorsed my selections -- a smoked-duck noodle soup and fried radish cakes with XO sauce -- with a welcome enthusiasm. 
The room was stark red and white, with high ceilings, marble-topped tables and exposed ductwork, and I slurped my noodles (smoked duck tastes surprisingly like really good ham) undisturbed.
After dinner (154 Hong Kong dollars), I heard from Fed. 
He and some friends were meeting in Lan Kwai Fong, Central's hopping night-life district; would I like to join?
Yes, I said, then changed my mind. 
There is something quite wonderful about walking the streets of a megalopolis at night, with lamps glowing in the apartments above and a million dramas taking place as people close up shop, get drunk, argue on cellphones, and neck quietly in the dark corners of empty office plazas.
Sunday morning brought a hunger that reminded me of when, at the age of 18 months (so my parents recount), I stood up in my chair at a slow-to-serve restaurant and cried out, ''I want Chinese food!
Give me Chinese food!''
No more fusion -- I wanted the classics. 
I wanted dim sum. 
Make that Dim Sum, a retro-traditional dumpling parlor 15 minutes' walk from the Cosmopolitan, past a series of cemeteries -- Muslim, Roman Catholic, Protestant, Parsee and Hindu -- whose multilingual tombstones reminded me of Hong Kong's tourism slogan: ''Asia's World City.''
Dim Sum was also directly across the street from Tim's apartment; he woke up just as I arrived and joined me for two kinds of shrimp dumplings, fried pork dumplings, roast pork buns, chive boxes and -- because I'd heard Calvin Trillin loves it -- sweet fried milk. 
The little plates fulfilled that 30-year-old hunger, but, since the bill was just 91 Hong Kong dollars each, left me with one last dilemma: How to spend the last 400 or so in my pocket before my flight?
Dim Sum's neighborhood, Tim informed me, happens to be known for its foot-massage parlors. 
The name Foot Joy intrigued me, and for the next 50 minutes (and for 198 Hong Kong dollars), my feet underwent a process that left them soft, limp and close to joyful.
In fact, they felt so good that before I knew it, I had walked back to Happy Valley, where a series of horse races from Macao were being projected on a video screen. 
(Live races run Wednesdays.) I paid my entry fee of 5 Hong Kong dollars, and split my last 200 between two horses: Sea Treasure, a sure thing at 3.4-1, and Oh Great, the 99-1 long shot. 
One minute 50.3 seconds later, it was time to go home.
Total amount spent: 2,760.80 Hong Kong dollars ($521).

text:

One of the indelible images in women's soccer history is Brandi Chastain's left-footed penalty kick past the Chinese goalkeeper Gao Hong to win the 1999 World Cup for the United States.
The goal was followed by a brouhaha about a doffed jersey and an exposed sports bra.
Now, less than two years later, Gao is tending goal for the New York Power, one of eight teams in the new Women's United Soccer Association, which opens next month and features nearly all of Chastain's teammates and four of Gao's from the Chinese national team.
Among Gao's new teammates for the 21-game W.U.S.A. season are Tiffeny Milbrett, Christie Pearce and Sara Whalen, all United States World Cup veterans, plus the elite Norwegian national team players Gro Espeseth and Ann Kristin Aarones.
"She never thought of the U.S. players as enemies, but she always tried her best to play a good game against them," Heike Chan, who translated for Gao, said yesterday at a W.U.S.A. news conference in Manhattan. 
"She likes the U.S. team. 
She's excited to be on the same team as Tiffeny. 
She sees her role is to promote soccer."
Gao has met the United States players on occasion, but her inability to speak English got in the way. 
"They could only smile at each other or pat each other on the shoulder," Chan said. 
"But even that she felt good about."
Milbrett said: "I have incredible respect for her. 
I hope to learn a lot more about her. 
We may not learn a lot soccer-wise, but to get inside her brain, to learn how she grew up and how she views life."
Gao knows a little English, but she will be taking language classes after the W.U.S.A. teams finish training next month in San Diego. 
Chan said that Gao knew of the league's startup plans well before she was signed last fall. 
"Her only surprise in coming here is in how well developed it is," Chan said.
W.U.S.A. officials have enormous confidence that they have produced an attractive, marketable mix by allocating United States team stars like Chastain, Milbrett, Mia Hamm, Brian Scurry and Julie Foudy to the eight teams, then adding elite international players and rising college stars.
They believe the W.U.S.A. is more immediately attractive than Major League Soccer, largely because of the United States team's success.
Power Coach Pat Farmer said that while there are other women's professional leagues, "This is the premier league for women."
The league also plans to inject its players into communities to build upon the large interest in their sport among soccer-playing girls and young women and their families.
"We have to get involved, do what we love to do," Milbrett said, "and show that we're not here just to play awesome soccer, but for the betterment of people around us."
The Power opens in Atlanta on April 21. 
The first home game, against the San Diego Spirit, will be played April 29 at Mitchel Athletic Complex in Uniondale, N.Y.

text:

For all her accomplishments as soccer's leading scorer and the biggest superstar in women's team sports, Mia Hamm has never sustained her brilliance consistently throughout a major tournament like the World Cup or the Olympics.
That may soon change. 
At 31, as she nears retirement after the 2004 Summer Games in Athens, Hamm is playing the most complete soccer of her career. 
She delivered a pair of goals and an assist tonight in a 5-0 victory over Nigeria before a crowd of 31,553 at Lincoln Financial Field, matching her goal output for the entire 1999 Women's World Cup and placing the United States on the verge of qualifying for this tournament's quarterfinals.
In the past, Hamm's confidence has been mercurial, rising or falling with her ability to put the ball into the net. 
She has scored only twice in the knockout phase of a World Cup or an Olympics. 
But she has become more assured, versatile and resilient -- no longer consumed by defeat or a failure to score -- during three seasons with the Washington Freedom in the Women's United Soccer Association.
As her teammates on the national team have become more accomplished and better known, Hamm no longer has an urgent obligation to carry the team on the field, or to shoulder the burden of media attention off it. 
Freed of the responsibility to take control, she seems more willing to do it.
In tonight's rugged game, Hamm tackled fiercely, tracked back to retrieve balls, dropped into midfield on occasion and seemed intently driven from the beginning.
"She wants the responsibility on her shoulders," Coach April Heinrichs said. 
"I believe this will be her best World Cup."
A reluctant superstar, Hamm now seems more comfortable with her celebrity and more relaxed in the way she plays. 
She has scored a pair of goals and collected four assists in two matches of this World Cup, her fourth. 
With 8 career goals and 12 assists, she has surpassed Michelle Akers of the United States and Sun Wen of China as the leading all-time scorer in the women's world championship.
"There's not a reluctance to take over games," the captain, Julie Foudy, said of Hamm. 
"Before, she wasn't reluctant, but she was content with others' taking the stage. 
Now, she's saying, 'I can do it.'
She's playing with an intensity that is inspiring all of us."
The United States (2-0) can advance to the quarterfinals with a draw or narrow defeat on Sunday against North Korea in Columbus, Ohio. 
In the first game of tonight's doubleheader, Sweden (1-1) defeated North Korea (1-1) by 1-0 as forward Victoria Svensson scored on a volley in the seventh minute.
The United States had defeated Nigeria by 7-1 in the 1999 World Cup as the match grew edgy and scabrous. 
The Americans expected a similar game tonight, and Nigeria quickly fell into trouble with its fierce tackling.
In the fifth minute, the Nigerian captain, Florence Omagbemi, took down forward Cindy Parlow from behind in the penalty area, and the Argentine referee, Florencia Romano, signaled a penalty kick.
As the game moved into the sixth minute, Hamm called for the kick, which was a departure from the 1999 World Cup final, when she had not wanted to take one -- then did reluctantly -- in the penalty kick shootout against China. 
Tonight, she assuredly placed a low shot inside the right post. 
The Nigerian goalkeeper, Precious Dede, guessed incorrectly, shuffling to her left, and Hamm pumped her fist in celebration at the 1-0 lead.
In the 12th minute, Parlow was fouled a second time, giving the United States a free kick from 32 yards. 
Again, Hamm stepped forward to take the kick. 
Playing in the W.U.S.A., she has refined her playmaking skills and fashioned herself into a dangerous threat on set pieces. 
Hamm intended to make a pass from the left flank as Parlow made a run toward the far post, but the ball kept floating inexorably toward the goal. 
Dede seemed frozen off her line and reached up with both hands but could not control the ball, allowing the United States to take a 2-0 lead.
Two minutes into the second half, Hamm placed a corner kick perfectly onto the head of Parlow, who was left unmarked from six yards out. 
Abby Wambach scored in the 65th minute, and Foudy delivered a penalty kick in the 89th minute, but the game was dominated by Hamm.
"It's more consistent than in the past," Hamm said. 
"I credit the W.U.S.A. for putting you under pressure week in and week out. 
I'm trying to enjoy this. 
I'm definitely a lot looser than in previous World Cups. 
I'm an intense, emotional person. 
Sometimes, stopping to smell the roses isn't a bad thing."
RUSSIA 3, GHANA 0
Marina Saenko got one goal and started another scoring play as Russia beat Ghana in Carson, Calif.
Saenko scored on a free kick in the 36th minute, Natalia Barbachina made the score 2-0 in the 54th minute, and Olga Letyushova capped the scoring with a close-range volley in the 80th minute.
Russia goalkeeper Alla Volkova, sometimes rushing to the top of the box to turn away scoring threats, was particularly effective when Ghana had breakaways.
CHINA 1, AUSTRALIA 1
Bai Jie scored in the 46th minute as heavily favored China settled for a tie with Australia in Carson, Calif.
Heather Garriock scored in the 28th minute to give the upstart Australians (1-0-1) a short-lived lead.
China (1-0-1), ranked fourth in the world to Australia's 15th, kept the pressure on most of the second half, but Australia's defense crowded back into its own zone to turn back repeated threats.

text:

It was only 24 minutes into BRAD DAVIS'S Major League Soccer career, but he quickly had the look of a grizzled, confident veteran.
Davis was inserted into Saturday's game in the 81st minute by MetroStars Coach OCTAVIO ZAMBRANO, replacing ROSS PAULE on the left side of the midfield. 
Davis scored the game-winning goal in overtime as the MetroStars defeated the Columbus Crew, 2-1.
"He obviously wanted me to take care of my role defensively," Davis said, referring to Zambrano. 
But he mostly wanted me to go forward and make things happen. 
I'm an offensive player. 
I had a couple of chances but couldn't put them away until the overtime.
Davis, who is 20 and played at St. Louis University, was picked by the MetroStars No. 3 over all in the recent M.L.S. draft. 
He showed his offensive prowess last year, scoring 10 goals and adding 14 assists as the Billikens advanced to the quarterfinals of the N.C.A.A. tournament.
Against the Crew (he had also been a late sub in a 1-0 loss to Columbus at Giants Stadium on April 3), Davis went immediately forward, forcing Columbus to scramble. 
Early in the second five-minute overtime period, Davis drifted into the left side of the penalty area as the MetroStars attacked on the right side.
"I don't remember who made the original run, but I do know I was calling for the ball because I was open on the opposite side from the get-go," Davis said. 
There were a couple of shots that were deflected. 
I held my position and, as it rolled to me, my eyes felt like they opened up real big. 
I put my head down and struck it well.
The game-winner, however, is no guarantee of more playing time.
"Hopefully, I will get more playing time," Davis said. 
"I feel I can play. 
It's just a matter of time."
WORLD CUP
BORA MILUTINOVIC, the peripatetic Serb who is the coach of China's national team, said that he might stay in China after the World Cup, but that he would definitely retire from coaching. 
"I'll be 60 when the World Cup is over," Milutinovic told a daily newspaper in Sichuan. 
"The places where I prefer to stay most are the United States and China, not Mexico, where my family lives now."
As the start of the tournament nears, Chinese officials have told the nation's clubs that 11 injured national team players will not be allowed to play in remaining league games, even if they are fit. 
Striker HAO HAIDONG (toe) and the captain and veteran midfielder MA MINGYU (knee) top the list of injured players. 
"If all the players are injured, I would go to the World Cup alone," Milutinovic said.
China has scheduled five warm-up matches -- the first is against South Korea on April 27 -- before it begins play on June 4 against Costa Rica in a first-round group that also includes Brazil and Turkey.
The Manchester United and Ireland midfielder ROY KEANE tore a hamstring in last week's Champions League match in Spain and will be out for at least six weeks. 
The Irish defender STEPHEN CARR, who plays in England for Tottenham Hotspur, has been slow to recover from a knee injury.
"The World Cup's gone, and it's now about getting myself fit and playing football again," Carr said on the club's Web site. 
"I found out last week, and it's a massive disappointment."
Portugal, which opens World Cup play against the United States on June 5, will be without the 22-year-old Benfica wing SIMAO SABROSA. 
Sabrosa, who has played 12 times for the Portuguese national team, underwent surgery on his left knee after he was injured in last week's exhibition loss to Finland. 
Arsenal of the English Premier League said it was prepared to allow its Japanese midfielder, JUNICHI INAMOTO, to leave the club and join his national team at the end of April. 
Arsenal signed Inamoto for $5.7 million from Gamba Osaka last summer, but he has been unable to win a spot in the Gunners' starting lineup.
Japan is scheduled to play host to Costa Rica (April 17), Honduras (April 29) and Slovakia (May 4) in warm-up matches.
A poll of 442 college students conducted by the South Korean magazine Vox found that the American short-track speedskater APOLO ANTON OHNO was the most unwelcome at the World Cup. 
Ohno was followed by OSAMA BIN LADEN, JAY LENO and BRIGITTE BARDOT.
Ohno won a gold medal at the Salt Lake Games when a South Korean skater was disqualified; Leno and Bardot have ridiculed South Koreans for their custom of eating dog.
CORNER KICKS
The New York Power of the Women's United Soccer League will play a benefit match at 7 tonight at Baker Field in Upper Manhattan against the Columbia University's women's team. 
The match will be preceded by a clinic at 5 p.m.
On Sunday, the Power defeated the Philadelphia Charge, 2-1, in an exhibition match at Indian Hills High School in Oakland, N.J.
The Power opens its second season on Saturday night in Washington against the Freedom.
